2583.prule: No contrastive stress; three-tone language (21/33/55). Default: the first syllable of the lexeme is stressed ('stem-initial prominence'), stated as typical and 'particularly' for disyllables of all word classes. In lexemes of three or more syllables the stress can instead fall on the second syllable, which the author attributes ('the data suggests... may', 'possibly') to the onset consonant of that syllable: /p/, /b/, /l/, /y/ attract the stress (ʃɩ̀ˈbátà 'poverty', kwàˈlálà 'elder', yàˈpɩ́lwà 'sheep', gʋ̀ˈbálá 'stone', zwàˈlɩ́yá 'husband', mɩ̀ˈyáhà 'goat', gùrˈbílə̀ 'he-goat', gàˈpʋ́nwà 'hyena') versus initial stress otherwise (ˈbàmbàlà 'bow', ˈlámtàlà 'bag', ˈpàkálà 'field', ˈbə̀lı́wé 'cow', ˈlàràwá 'elephant', ˈyáláká 'day', ˈbámáká 'antelope', ˈpàhàkà 'law'). The tone-bearing unit (henceforth TBU) is the syllable' (p. 66); few minimal pairs (Newman/Newman 1974: 113: tonally distinguished words 'probably represent less than 5% of the words in the language'); contour tones non-tonemic. 'pitch is distinctive in Nʋngʋrama, while stress is not' (p. 70). fn. 105 (p. 71) carries Newman/Newman 1974: 113: no downdrift and little pitch variation lead them to suggest 'that Longuda may be developing into a pitch-accent language'. Pike 1982 fn. 9 (excerpt in the copy consulted, second-hand) reports Newman & Newman 1974 as finding 'some close correlation between stress and high pitch, so that the first high tone syllable in a word is the stressed syllable'. Vigeland's own examples do not separate the two accounts: all eight peninitial-stress examples are L-H(-x) with the first H on the stressed syllable, while three initial-stress examples (ˈpàkálà L-H-L, ˈbə̀lı́wé L-H-H, ˈlàràwá L-L-H) contradict the Newmans' tone-linked rule.

2589.prule: Penultimate stress as the dominant ('most common') pattern, quantity-insensitive, counted from the right edge: the first syllable in disyllables, 'the second from the last syllable' in trisyllables; stress is noncontrastive (1993: 59). Words of four or more syllables: no statement in 1994; the 1993 transcriptions show penult ([ˌnɔkə'siŋud] 'to have smelled', [ˌmɔmə'lɔkɔŋ] 'transplant rice seedlings') and final ([ˌʔiŋgarə'nan] 'called'). Unstressed /a/, /ɔ/ reduce to [ə] in words of three or more syllables (both sources).

2591.dq: In a Tanana word with more than one stress, one stress is promoted to the status of Head of Prosodic Word and bears stronger stress. In Salcha and Minto, the head of a prosodic word is the rightmost stressed syllable. In both dialects, compound and phrasal stress is also rightmost. (p.218; the word-position duration test on p.218 excludes phrase-final syllables 'to avoid confusion from phrase-fin…

2591.heavy: 'Heavy syllables are those which contain full vowels or are closed by a consonant' (p.189); 'I will claim that Tanana reduced vowels are underlyingly associated with one mora, and full vowels with two moras' and 'C@ is a light syllable, but Ca is a heavy syllable; however, C@C is also heavy' (p.195, @ = schwa; weight by position, Hayes 1989); codas do not make syllables superheavy beyond two moras (p.196). The vowel half of the criterion is the full-vs-reduced quality contrast, which the source represents as bimoraic vs monomoraic. Weight decides only which non-stem syllables are stressed: the stem is stressed regardless of weight and non-tonal heavy suffixes are stressless (Nonfinality >> WSP).
2591.dflt: Every word contains a stem, which is stressed regardless of weight (Associate-Stem >> Foot-Binarity, 'Stressed light stems', table (48) p.222); in an all-light disyllabic stem the first syllable is stressed (LL trochee, e.g. Salcha 'sheep' (16) p.197); in strings of light prefix syllables the first of two open reduced-vowel syllables is stressed, counted leftward from the stem, and a leftover single light syllable is unfooted (21) p.201.
2591.prule: Word (primary) stress is the rightmost stressed syllable, and which syllables count as stressed is decided by morphology before weight: every stem is stressed, even a light one (Associate-Stem); every lexically tonal suffix or enclitic is stressed (Associate-Tone); non-tonal suffixes and enclitics are unstressed even when heavy. So main stress falls on the stem when the stem is word-final and on a following tonal suffix otherwise (Minto possessive -a' takes word stress; Salcha, whose suffixes are toneless, keeps it on the rightmost stem). Compound and phrasal stress are likewise rightmost. Duration is the chief acoustic correlate; the position is not computable from syllable count.
2591.srule: All stressed syllables other than the rightmost (promoted) one are lesser stresses ('basic stress'). Stressed are: every stem, even when light; every heavy syllable (full vowel or closed syllable), adjacent heavies each stressed; lexically tonal suffixes/enclitics; and in strings of light (open, reduced-vowel) prefix syllables the heads of moraic trochees built leftward from the stem foot, so a light syllable is stressed only before another light syllable, never immediately before the stem, and a single leftover light syllable is unstressed. Non-tonal suffixes/enclitics are unstressed even when heavy; a non-final stem keeps a lesser stress when a tonal suffix (or, in compounds, a later member) carries word stress. In connected speech all but the strongest stress may be reduced but stay durationally distinct.

tn.translation: As regards the tonetics of the Luba-Katanga discussed here, it hardly deviates from the general rules Burssens established for Luba-Kasayi. The mid tone mostly turns out to function merely as a variant of one of the monotonemes: high vs. low, both grammatically and semantically, so that the role of the dynamic intensity accent, as in Luba-Kasayi, is pushed back to a subordinate level. Finally the author devotes a well-documented survey to the influence tonemes and prosodemes can exert on the syntactic units.

2595.heavy: Not relevant to main-stress placement. For the secondary grades Wiklund counts a syllable long 'natura oder positione' (long vowel/diphthong, or closed by a consonant cluster, §20.2c), and a short first syllable entails a long second (§33).
2595.prule: Main stress (hauptton, fortis) on the first syllable of the word in words of every length (2-5 syllables listed explicitly in §20.2-4; general statement §21). Syllable quantity plays no role in placing the main stress; it only grades the secondary stresses. Corroborated verbatim by Wiklund 1901 §17 'Accenten ligger i lapskan alltid på ordets första stafvelse' and Collinder 1938 §141 'Der hauptdruck ruht auf dem ersten lauttal.'
2595.srule: Two grades of secondary stress, levis (strong) and levior (weak), placed by syllable quantity and rhythm after the initial main stress: disyllables have none when the 1st syllable is long and the 2nd short, levis on the 2nd when the 1st is short (so the 2nd long), levior on the 2nd when both are long; trisyllables levior on the 3rd when the 2nd is short, levis on the 2nd when the 1st is short, levior on the 2nd when the first two are long; in four- and five-syllable words levis/levior mostly on every following long syllable and also on the 3rd and 5th syllables when the 4th is short; in sum a secondary stress can fall on any non-initial syllable, with the 1st, 3rd, 5th counted as stressed and the 2nd, 4th as unstressed (§21). Restated by Wiklund 1901/1915 §17 (one or more 'biaccenter'; a long vowel in the 2nd or 4th syllable carries one) and, for Gällivare Forest Saami, Collinder 1938 §§143-147 (long syllables stronger; rhythmic odd-syllable tendency).

2597.prule: Free (lexically fixed, non-demarcative) stress accent, reconstructed: its position is 'not reducible to first/last syllable' (Hyman criterion A, scored Y for Lycian in Billing 2026) and distinguishes disyllabic a-stems of the same shape (Lyc. A tama- 'building', initial accent, vs. hrm̃ma- 'temenos', final accent; lãta- 'dead person' vs. xñta- 'trust'); accent is 'largely columnar, non-mobile' within paradigms, with 'some cases of possible mobile accent' (trqqas vs. trqqñti 'Storm-God', after Kloekhorst 2013:143; also Kloekhorst's mãhãi vs. mahãna). The Lycian alphabet does not mark accent; placement is recovered only negatively (a syncopated vowel or a syllabic resonant m̃/ñ was unaccented), so every statement is a diachronic reconstruction, and Melchert 2004:596 warns that the syncope-based accounts risk circularity and are 'not remotely definitive'. No fixed position and no weight sensitivity is claimed by any source.
2597.srule: Not described in Billing 2023 (all slides), Billing 2026 Oxford handout (all) or Billing 2026 'Recovering' (slides 1-28). Il y a quatre tonèmes en lyèlé: haut / ́ /, bas / ̀ /, moyen / ̄ / (marqué par une absence de marque de ton); les tonèmes ponctuels sont susceptibles de se combiner entre eux pour donner des tonèmes modulés, bas-haut / ̌ / et haut-bas / ̂ /. ... Le ton, à ce moment, indique uniquement le ton de la syllabe. Exemples: tonème haut ... ló " verser " tonème bas ... lò " homme " tonème moyen ... lo " casser " tonème bas-haut ... lŏ " liane "
tn.translation: Lyèlé is a tone language, i.e. a language that uses the melodic pitch of the voice for distinctive purposes. There are four tonemes in Lyèlé: high, low, mid (marked by the absence of a tone mark); the level tonemes can combine with one another to give modulated tonemes, low-high and high-low. ... The tone [mark] then indicates only the tone of the syllable. Examples: high toneme ló 'pour', low toneme lò 'man', mid toneme lo 'break', low-high toneme lŏ 'liana'.

2600.heavy: Heavy = bimoraic ('a syllable containing two morae', p. 135; 'A heavy syllable is branching'): long-vowel (CVV) and closed (CVC) syllables, cf. the endorsed McIntosh 1984:20 formulation 'the last non-final CVC or CVV syllable'; worked examples use CVC (kor-, -rol), CVV (-naa, -taa-) and CVVC (-waan-) as heavy. Light = one mora (CV).
2600.dflt: first syllable of the word ('If there are no heavy syllables the stress falls on the first syllable of the word', p. 133; pamarol 'small' -> initial, the heavy final -rol being extrametrical)
2600.prule: Unbounded quantity-sensitive rule: primary stress falls on the last (rightmost) heavy = bimoraic syllable of the word; in nominals the final syllable (normally the noun-class suffix) is extrametrical and never stressed, so the rule applies to the last non-final heavy syllable; in verbal words the final syllable counts. If the word has no (countable) heavy syllable, stress falls on the first syllable. Examples: korsuɗo 'cherished one' -> KOR.su.[ɗo]; rawaandu 'dog' -> ra.WAAN.[du]; pamarol 'small' -> PA.ma.[rol] (heavy final extrametrical); calminanaa 'you should greet for' -> stress on final -naa; dillintaako 'can't move' -> penult -taa-.
2600.srule: Secondary stress on heavy syllables (theory-internal, from the metrical analysis): each heavy (bimoraic) syllable heads a left-headed, quantity-sensitive, unbounded foot and every foot head 'receives (secondary) stress'; the head of the last foot takes the word stress, so all heavy syllables before the primary-stressed one carry secondary stress (final syllable of nominals extrametrical; a word with no heavy syllable is one foot, no secondary stress). Shown only in metrical trees (dillintaako: feet dil | lin | taa-ko, word stress on -taa-, p. 136); no phonetic evidence or marked transcriptions of secondary stress are given.

2600.tone: 'Unlike most of its neighbouring African languages, Fulfulde is not a tone language. Fulfulde does make use of intonation patterns.' (p. 137, endorsing Arnott 1970a:62 'Fula is an intonational rather than a tonal language'). Stress is realized by amplitude plus a pitch change whose direction follows sentence intonation; in declaratives the stressed syllable of a non-focused word shows a pitch drop, which Breedveld argues led Arnott 1965 and Noye 1974 to mis-hear the preceding high-pitched syllable (usually initial) as stressed. A word in isolation gets declarative intonation, so citation forms show H on the initial syllable and L on the stressed one (rawaandu, daneejum, janngirde).

2601.tone: Two basic tones (bas, haut) plus falling and rising 'tons doubles'; tones marked with acute / circumflex / inverted circumflex, low unmarked; minimal pairs (20a) moto 'être humain' vs motó 'tête', nguba vs ngúba 'bouclier/arachide'; tonal minimal pairs also grammatical (20b). Tone rules pp. 23–26: contraction (H-H>H, H-B>D, B-B>B, B-H>M), neutralisation and spreading ('le ton haut de la dernière syllabe d’un mot se propage sur la première syllabe du mot suivant' after elision), faille and élévation (BBH, HBB contexts; De Boeck 1951: 909 'tons doubles courts'; 'ces phénomènes sont rares'), tonal harmony (connective -a, TAM formatives take the prefix tone), tonal contrast (negative -to-, -i), metatony ('plutôt syntaxique': H of infinitive final -a lowered phrase-finally). On stress/accent the work is silent: a full-text search of the whole work for accent/intensité/pénultième/stress/proéminence/dynamique/prosod hits only the diacritic names on p. 22, the adverb class 'Intensité' p. 75 and a 'prosodique' in the comparative conclusions. Vowel length p. 16: 'On ne peut donc pas parler de longueur vocalique proprement dite quoique certaines séquences de voyelles restent encore difficiles à expliquer'; long syllables (VV, CVV) arise only from vowel contraction and this 'n’affecte pas la more de la syllabe en Mbenga' (p. 26). No penultimate lengthening or prominence remark.

2602.prule: Lexical, Portuguese-type right-edge stress. 2603.dq: Im allgemeinen werden die Wörter im Kimashami auf der vorletzten, seltener auf der drittletzten Silbe betont. Ist dagegen die letzte Silbe eines Wortes lang ... dann erhält diese den Ton.
2603.dloc: Vorwort, p. VII, last paragraph before 'Zum Schluß...' / 'Der Verfasser.' (listed as 'Betonung' in the Inhaltsverzeichnis, p. IX); Google Books page-id RA2-PR7 (page scan held); context pp. V-VI (RA2-PR5, RA2-PR6).
2603.heavy: 'die letzte Silbe eines Wortes lang, was durch einen Strich über dem Endvokal ausgedrückt ist' — a final syllable whose vowel is long (macron-marked: ā ē ī ō ū; the Vorwort derives several of these long finals from contraction, e.g. shikabō < shikabwaa, and the future ending -ā in shikabā). Only vowel length is named; nothing about closed syllables (the language has open syllables in the examples).
2603.prule: Word stress falls in general on the penultimate syllable, more rarely on the antepenultimate; if the final syllable is long (a long vowel, written with a macron over the final vowel, e.g. kū 'alt', rū 'umsonst', kō 'jung', kufī 'nahe', shikabō, shikabā), the final syllable bears the stress instead.
2603.srule: Not mentioned in Augustiny 1914 (Vorwort, Aussprache pp. V-VII incl. the 'Betonung' paragraph p. VII; p. 52 tone remark): the two-sentence Betonung remark gives only the main-stress rule.

2603.tone: Augustiny 1914 himself recognises lexical tone: p. 52, sec. 45 Anm. 3, 'Viele Wörter, die ähnlich klingen, aber verschiedene Bedeutung haben, unterscheiden sich nur durch den Ton, Hoch-, Mittel- und Tiefton... Im Text sind die Tonzeichen weggelassen' (three-way high/mid/low; marks defined: vertical stroke above the syllable = high, below = low, mid unmarked; omitted in the running text, though the sec. 46 word list on the same page still prints them on homograph pairs, e.g. mbwà 'der Regen' vs mbwą 'die Nase'). His Vorwort 'Betonung' paragraph (p. VII) is a separate, positional word-stress statement ('erhält diese den Ton' there = takes the stress; note the loose terminology, 'Ton' serving for both stress and pitch). All modern first-hand work treats Machame/Mashami as a tone language and states no stress rule: Yukawa 1989 (A tonological study of Machame verbs, ILCAA; H vs L, falling tone only word-final), Philippson & Montlahuc 2003 (Kilimanjaro Bantu; tone shift, surface SH/H/L), Rugemalira 2014 (tone-marked noun data). None denies word stress.

evidence_works.note: Comparative thesis. For Mashami itself it gives only tone data: a table of the four Common Bantu tone schemes (BB, HB, BH, HH) preserved in Gweno and Mashami, e.g. Wama 'viande' (BB), múWi 'manche' (HB), mmbá 'maison' (BH), Ngúkú 'poulet' (HH), pp.446-447. Its prosodic claims are made for Chaga as a group and worked out on the Vunjo dialect after McHugh 1990: 'Le chaga (de même que des langues voisines, comme le kamba) est une langue où jouent en même temps un système tonal entièrement distinctif et un système d'accent démarcatif, les effets des deux s'entrecroisant' (p.288, footnote 1 crediting McHugh 1990 on Vunjo and Winter 1987 on Mochi); nominals leave the lexicon 'avec une syllabe accentuée (soit la pénultième, soit la finale)' (p.288); the penultimate accent is 'de loin la plus nombreuse', final accent belongs to monosyllables and contracted stems, where 'le processus de coalescence vocalique ua > o... aboutit finalement à accentuer la finale' (pp.385-386); in the typology Chaga is listed under 'langues à culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième (langues à prosodèmes distinctifs, mais sans opposition de longueur)' (p.483); Annexe Vunjo: 'langue tonale, avec accent lexical partiellement libre', 'accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)' (pp.512-513). The Vunjo nominal data are cited with the author's own caveat 'mes informations sont insuffisantes' (p.384 n.1). No Mashami stress statement; no instrumental measurement.

Cada grupo intensivo está constituido de dos a veinte sílabas y se puede encontrarlo precedido y seguido de silencio. Lleva un solo acento principal.' -- the stress rule is stated over a 2-20-syllable pause-bounded stress group, not the gramma…
2604.dloc: sec. 1.2.3 'El Acento', p.11; sec. 1.1.3 'El acento' and sec. 1.2 'Distribución', p.9; sec. 1 'Los fonemas', p.5; endnotes 8-9, p.33
2604.prule: Stress is phonemic (a 'fonema de acento' proven by segmentally identical minimal pairs paníro/pániro, samáni/sámani, ikyianakyéro/ikyianákyero) and confined to a right-edge window: the single primary stress of the stress group falls most often on the penult or antepenult; on the final syllable only in the emphatic vocative; often on the pre-antepenult when that syllable is the first member of a vowel sequence; a few words have it elsewhere (pishimáatakye). No weight, sonority or morphological rule is stated.
2604.srule: Secondary stresses exist but their placement is not analysed: 'También aparecen acentos secundarios, los cuales... no se consideran según la colocación del acento principal. Se necesita un estudio más detallado' (Snell 1978 [1974] p.9; note 8 p.33 defers the definition and distribution of the stresses to future research). No later opened work (Snell 1998/2008, 2011; Chineri et al. 2020; Chen 2019; O'Hagan 2018) says anything about secondary stress.
2604.quote: 1.2.3. El Acento. El acento principal aparece con más frecuencia en la sílaba penúltima o antepenúltima del grupo intensivo. 2605.prule: Stress is non-contrastive and falls on the last syllable of the (phonological) word. Stated as fact for the four Transanfranciscan (Maxakalían-Krenák) varieties the authors have recordings/transcriptions by trained linguists for -- Maxakalí, Maxakalí Ritual (= Língua dos Cantos Rituais = the 19th-c. Makuní/Macuni dialect complex per Nikulin 2020:18), Pataxó-Hãhãhãe, Krenák -- and extended by speculation to Malalí. quantity-insensitive, final: computable from syllable count.
2605.srule: Not mentioned in Silva & Nikulin 2021 (Cadernos de Etnolinguística 9(1): e090107), sec. 2 Fonologia p. 8 -- the work's only stress remark (non-contrastive, word-final) says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.

Soma-se a isso o fato de que a maior parte dos acentos diacríticos presentes nos registros do Malalí se encontram na última vogal da palavra.

2606.exq_: Las pocas palabras que ocurren sólo con tono bajo no tienen acento perceptible. [...] Todas las palabras de una sílaba con tono alto tienden a deslizarse a tono bajo.
2606.tone: Bosquejo §2.3.1: two phonemic tones, high /V́/ and low /V̀/; more than one H per phonological word possible; the only mention of 'acento' in the whole sketch is that all-L words 'no tienen acento perceptible', i.e. prominence is read off H tone. Optional phonetic glides: slight rise on a word-initial L before H; fall on a word-final H; monosyllabic H words glide to L with slight lengthening. Ardila 1995 (Forma y Función 8, p.125 and Macuna summary p.128): 'En barasana y macuna toda palabra lleva por lo menos un tono alto; no se presenta el patrón bajo-bajo' and 'Todas las palabras llevan por lo menos un tono alto' (partly contradicting the Bosquejo's 'pocas palabras' with only L). Dictionary 1993 p.5: 'La principal diferencia entre los subgrupos es la posición del acento en las palabras' -- accent position varies by clan-lect, no rule given. Barnes 1999 (Amazonian Languages, p.212, second-hand family survey) lists Macuna among Tucano languages that 'may have two or more contiguous high-pitched syllables, all of these syllables being equally accented'.

2609.prule: No stress rule stated. The thesis has no stress or prosody section, no stress-marked transcriptions and no placement statement; the single bearing remark (sec. 2.3.1.3, on non-phonemic vowel length) presupposes word-level primary stress with which long vowels 'generally coincide', 'hence their preponderance in word initial syllables' -- an implied, hedged word-initial tendency. The same paragraph says long vowels sit on 'the first syllable of a morpheme, even if embedded within a complex word', and the example the author calls typical, buy-a:ynju-wa 'you go and get', carries its length on the word's second (root-initial) syllable, so the implied system may equally be morpheme-initial as in sister language Kamu (Harvey 1989 sec. 2.12). Undecidable between fixed word-initial and morpheme-initial primary stress; flag 'implied initial, low confidence' for the rule-grade audit, pending a primary source.
